I feel that precisely because we have avoided such confrontations we are permitting responsible politicians everywhere to arrive at the conclusion which we on this side of the house have reached, namely that time is on our side.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 4, consideration in committee of BUI No. C-243, to amend the National Defence Act and other acts in consequence thereof-Mr. Hellyer -Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: When the committee rose last evening clause 2 was being considered. Shall clause 2 carry?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am entering into this debate because of my conviction that the proposal placed before us by the government is unsound and should be resisted.
I begin by expressing my regret that in our centennial year we should be involved in a debate such as this. During centennial year we are emphasizing the history and traditions of our country in every hamlet, community and city of Canada. We are drawing attention to a glorious past; we are recognizing the activities of our forefathers and paying tribute to their work in developing this country.
During centennial year we are also recognizing the devotion to duty and the sacrifices of generations of military people who have contributed over the years to the defence of this country. During that historical survey attention will be drawn to the early conflicts in the early settlement of this country. Attention will be drawn to the difficulties with the native population, to the struggle with the United States in 1812-14, to the Fenian raids which caused loss of life and disturbance on our borders, to the 1885 rebellion in western Canada, to Canadian participation in the South African war, the first world war, the
14554	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment second world war and in Korea; and yet during this year when these things are going on, and when this recognition is being given to those who devoted their lives to the service of their country, we are caught in a conflict instituted by the Minister of National Defence, and supported by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Prime Minister, with regard to the military services of our country. And if the government's proposal is carried, the traditions of these fighting services will be wiped out.
I say, Mr. Chairman, it is with regret that in this centennial year we have to have a debate of this nature. I do not normally shrink too rapidly from mild controversy in the House of Commons, but I do confess it is with great reluctance that in this particular year, at this particular time, I find myself involved in opposition to the government on an issue such as this. Just this coming week end, sir, there will be a celebration here in Ottawa, and one in France at Vimy Ridge, recognizing the activities of Canadian military people in the first world war. It is proper that this should be done.
The Vimy Ridge ceremony will bring back to the knowledge of Canadians who lived in that period, and to the attention of the younger generation, the sacrifices and endeavour of people in the first world war. Their attention will be drawn to the battle of Vimy Ridge, which was not more severe than other battles in that war, and did not occasion greater proportionate loss of life than some of the other battles in that war. It was not greater in importance than, say, the gas attack at Saint Julien, or the battle of the Somme, or the Passchendaele struggle in the fall of 1917, or the 100 days of victorious advance in 1918; but the capture of Vimy Ridge, one of the strongest points on the western front in 1914 to 1918, marked a change in the difficulties of the allied armies on that front, and was about the only optimistic note struck in the year 1917, during which we almost lost the war. It was the good fortune of the Canadian corps, working together, to be the spearhead of that attack, and Canada on that occasion found her national identity. For 50 years I have been wondering at people who are bemoaning the fact that we are striving to discover our national identity. It was discovered then, on April 9, 1917-

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
-when between 80,000 and 90,000 young Canadians played their part in that struggle, and when in the space of three

DEBATES	April 5, 1967
days over 3,000 of them were killed and over 7,000 were wounded. Sir, with these ceremonies so close to us I say again it is with regret I have to engage in a debate on the situation concerning the services for which I have such a high regard, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.
It has been my good fortune to see these forces in action or to be assisted by them somewhere along the line in the course of such military experience as I have had, and I have nothing but admiration for the two forces with which I did not serve, the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force. I have the greatest respect for the fighting men in those services, as well as for those in the army, and the greatest regret that they are facing this crisis at this period of our history when the government is attempting to wipe out their great past and launch out on an uncharted future without placing reliance on the experience gained by the fighting men of Canada over the last 100 years.
Sir, this is exactly what is going to happen. Section 15 of the present statute, which is called the National Defence Act, reads as follows:
The Canadian Forces are the naval, army and air forces of Her Majesty raised by Canada and consist of three services, namely, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.
We are being asked in this parliament to strike out that section and substitute the following for it:
The Canadian Forces are the armed forces of Her Majesty raised by Canada and consist of one service called the Canadian Armed Forces.
We are being asked to strike out the three services, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force and substitute for them the Canadian Armed Forces. The identity of the three well known services will be destroyed. We will have one single force and, if the minister has his way, dressed in the same uniform with a common rank structure.
That is what is facing us in this debate and that is what we are objecting to, among other things that are in the proposed amendments. I certainly lodge my objection to the formation of a single force to be simply called the Canadian Armed Forces, and to the destruction of the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force.


Yesterday, sir, attention was drawn once again to the lack of confidence that we have in the Minister of National Defence. The hon. member for Calgary North indicated, with several examples tied down to evidence given, that the minister is an unreliable purveyor of information to the House of Commons, and I raised a question of privilege on that occasion in order to underline the seriousness of the situation. I do not propose to spend all my time on that aspect of the subject today, but I do intend to draw attention to the credibility gap which has developed between the minister and the House of Commons, and between the minister and the Canadian people, and to point out that that gap has become a yawning gulf separating us, because we can no longer rely on the Minister of National Defence.
I think it is destructive of the parliamentary system that we are not able to rely upon statements by ministers of the crown. If we cannot rely upon their statements, what type of government have we in this democracy? It is no longer a democracy if ministers of the crown fail to give us the facts and fail to give us the absolute truth.
I drew attention to this difficulty on November 4 last in a speech which was not widely reported. In fact I do not think it was reported at all, but I make no complaint. I am not attacking the press of this country as the minister did. I think the press representatives of this country achieve miracles in interpreting some of the things we say here in the House of Commons, considering the restriction of space that they have in their newspapers and the, shall I say, domineering attitude taken by their editors, as a result of which some of their best copy ends up in the waste paper basket instead of in the columns of the newspapers. I am sure that is where most of the reports of my speeches end up. I do not blame the reporters at all. I find no fault with them for that. They really do a good job of summarizing in a short space what perhaps takes several hours to say here in the House of Commons or in committee. However, my speech of November 4 was a speech which showed that the Minister of National Defence was misleading the house and the country.

The minister replied: "Not yet, Mr. Speaker." Then we went on to talk about the walking-out uniform, and I asked:

National Defence Act Amendment 1966. These all are senior officers-commodores, rear admirals and vice admirals in the navy; brigadiers, major generals and lieutenant generals in the army, and air commodores, air vice marshals and air marshals in the air force. Of a total of 79 officers, 21 were from the navy, 28 from the army and 30 from the air force. Of the total, 38 were normal retirements by reason of age and 41 were either compulsorily retired or submitted their resignations before their term was up. The outstanding example was Lieutenant General Moncel who had between five and six years remaining before he would reach normal retirement age. Yet, the minister had told us away back in July 1966 that the officers did not leave. He said:
I told them I respected their rights to disagree and I made it clear that they could leave with full honours. None did.
We do not know whether that means that none did leave or that none left with full honours. I suppose there is something extra in that to consider. These were not the only officers who left. On February 13 of this year, at page 12938 of Hansard, a return was given with regard to a question asked by the hon. member for Halifax concerning resignations of serving officers of the Canadian forces at national defence headquarters. It is an astonishing list. It shows that 264 officers left national defence headquarters, 56 of them because of age and 208 because of retirement, voluntary or compulsory. These are officers most of whom are below the ranks I mentioned a little while ago.
So, what credibility can one place in this minister? Those two examples are not anything like as serious as the third example I now present to the house. This will be found in No. 16 of the proceedings of the committee on national defence for Thursday, February 9, at pages 651 and 652. I asked the minister certain questions, and I should like to read what I said:
I would like to have It proved to this committee that unification will provide the necessary reduction in overhead personnel operating and maintenance costs so that that will come down to 75 per cent and that there will be 25 per cent available for capital expenditures. The reason for my wanting proof of it is that we have been hearing for three years that great savings will be made by unification. What is the evidence? I am not talking about integration; I am talking about unification.
Then Mr. Hellyer replied:
I do not think anyone has made the statement- certainly I have not-that the financial savings from unification itself would be very great, or that they would be easy to document.

Well, I looked back at the white paper. I submit to you, sir, that the centennial celebrations in the year 2067, in addition to Magna Carta, the British North America Act and the Canadian Bill of Rights, there will also be on display for the people of that time the white paper of 1964, one of the great historic documents in Canadian history. I keep reading this document-the white paper -almost every week; it is becoming very worn. At page 19 of that white paper this is what the minister wrote:
Sufficient savings should accrue from unification to permit a goal of 25 per cent of the budget to be devoted to capital equipment being realized in the years ahead.
During the committee hearings the minister told me that no such statement ever had been made.

One can obtain a copy of the speech of December 7, with a red cover. It was a special publication which cost over $5,000 and was distributed widely across the country. It is a historical document which will be worth a lot of money 100 years from now. In that speech the minister gave four fundamental reasons for the importance of a single unified force. I had occasion to deal with those four reasons during discussions of the defence committee. I felt that the best person to deal with them would be Lieut. Gen. Guy Simonds. I think most military men in the country will agree that he is the outstanding officer from the army during our period who is now living.

General Simonds belongs to our period. He enjoyed a good career and gained very wide experience during the second world war. He continued with the forces after, and became chief of the general staff. I do not know of anybody who has greater knowledge of actual warfare than General Simonds, particularly in respect of the combined operations of the navy, army and air force.
General Simonds has wider experience than anyone I know with staff colleges, and in respect of the theoretical side of warfare. He
National Defence Act Amendment also has a great deal of managerial experience which he gained while here at Ottawa and as chief of the general staff. It was my feeling that he was the best person to answer questions in respect of the four fundamental reasons for having a single unified service. I put questions to him and he supplied answers.
The first fundamental reason the minister gave us in that celebrated speech is this:
With the establishment of a common identity: sailors, soldiers, and airmen, although loyal to their ships, regiments and squadrons, will have an overriding loyalty to the whole force and its total objectives on behalf of Canada.
Those are the minister's words and that is the first argument. I then asked General Simonds this question:
Do you consider that under the triservice system there has been a lack of an overriding loyalty to Canada?
The general then replied:
X most certainly was never conscious of any during my service. I think that going back to the war and after, the Canadian serviceman was very proud of his country and very loyal to it. I do not think you could have demanded a higher degree of loyalty.
The second fundamental reason advanced by the minister was under the heading, "Careers". The minister said:
For able and highly-motivated individuals, both officers and other ranks, wider, more challenging and rewarding carreer opportunities will be available.
Unification will provide better and fairer employment prospects for service personnel. Under a system of separate services, opportunities are naturally limited to the scope, tasks and requirements of the individual service.
I then asked the general:
Do you see a substantial improvement in career opportunities that could result only from unification?
The general then replied:
I personally cannot.
This man has as wide experience as anyone in Canada. The third fundamental reason the minister advanced is this:
The unified force will provide much greater flexibility to meet changing requirements in defence organization made necessary by advances in military technology and changes in the international situation.
I then asked the general:
Do you consider that a unified force is essential to make it adaptable to changes in military technology and in the international situation?

He replied:
One of our problems, certainly in the army, and I think it affected people in the other services, was as the services tend to become more and more technical, getting a man of the necessary basic foundation of education to make him even good at one thing, and getting really thoroughly trained in one field.
The fourth basic fundamental reason the minister gave is this:
The nature of modern warfare has resulted in a compaction of time and distance to the point where decision making and reaction time must be much swifter than ever before in history. A unified force best meets this demand.
The need for fast decision making and quick reaction is synonymous with modern warfare.
I then asked the general this question:
Now, I do not know of anyone who has greater experience than yourself in the demands of modern warfare, decision making, quick reaction and the co-ordination of combined operations. Do you consider that the demands of modern warfare require a single service concept or, in other words, unification?
Then general then said:
No, I do not believe it does.
The general then gave a lengthy explanation as to why he had come to that conclusion. Those are the four fundamental reasons given by the minister in support of unification.

Thank you very much. I thank the minister for external affairs. I am glad that he is in his seat because I intend to say something about him very soon. I will also have something to say about the Prime Minister before I conclude, unless I am interrupted.
It was brought out time and time again in evidence before the committee that the reason for having a defence force was to train men to fight, in the event our country was attacked or our people were in danger. That is the fundamental reason and that is why they are combat forces. All the supply services, all the administrative services, all the command structure are designed in order that the combat forces may be able to play their part effectively in battle, whether it is on our
[Mr. Churehill.l

own shores, which God forbid, or whether it is further abroad, in Europe or somewhere else in the world.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
When our forces are fighting abroad, as they were in the two great wars and in Korea, they were protecting our way of life and protecting the people of Canada; but they were doing it miles distant from our country, and we were saved from the destruction of our country. I believe we are the most fortunate country in the world; we have been saved from awful destruction from artillery Are, missiles and bombing up to this point, and I hope we will be in the future. It pays dividends to conduct your battles far afield, whether it is with the navy thousands of miles from our shore or whether it is with the air force and army abroad fighting on some other continent.
Our defence forces-we call them defence forces-exist for that purpose, namely to have combat people ready for action. Canada takes second place to no country in the world when it comes to combat forces. This was proved in the first world war, in the second world war and in Korea. Let me remind the people of this country that following the assault on Vimy Ridge, which will be commemorated in just a few days now, the Canadian Corps was recognized by our opponents, the Germans, by General Ludendorf himself, as shock troops. Wherever Canadians appeared in the field of battle in 1917 and 1918 the Germans were alarmed, and with justification, because every time the Canadian Corps did appear in those last 18 months of the war, the Germans lost very, very heavily; they lost ground, they lost men, they lost artillery, they lost everything-and they finally lost the war. We were shock troops on a par with the best troops of England, the Guards, and on a par with the troops from Australia who fought side by side with us on some occasions.

speechtext: Why don't you write a book about it?

I may write a book about it some day, and I will correct some of the fallacious information that has been spread out to our Canadian people. I say this is what our defence forces exist for-combat forces; and all these supply services assist. You do not put them all together, as the minister is attempting to do, and neglect, as he is doing, the combat forces. That is what he is doing; he is neglecting the combat forces. The minister has his mind centred on the administrative and supply services. Of course they are
April 5. 1967	COMMONS
vital in wartime; you have to have them. A great many people have to serve behind the lines, behind the front or in the factories at home to provide the fighting troops with the arms and ammunition that they need. I hold these people in respect. But you cannot win a war just with the administrative and supply services. It is the combat forces that win a war. The minister fails to see this and is attempting to change the role of our combat forces.
Let us go by experience, without living in the past. I am so far ahead of the minister in this regard that I had him admit in committee-I wish I had the reference here today and had the time to give it-that I was a great proponent, as I always have been, of mobility in our forces. As far back as 12 or 14 years ago, right in this House of Commons, I demanded the mobility for our army which the minister is only now getting around to supplying; and he still has not completed it. He is so slow in this regard.
We were told that the minister discovered the armoured personnel carrier. I had the interesting experience of pointing out to him in the committee that the armoured personnel carrier was used in the second world war. The idea originated with General Simonds, and I, along with a few hundred other people, had the job of working out the tactics for it and using it on the battlefield. The minister thinks that he discovered the armoured personnel carrier. This is a Canadian "first" in the methods of dealing with infantry forces on the field of battle. We were the discoverers of the armoured personnel carrier. I am glad that the minister is gradually catching up with the second part of the twentieth century.
In our war experience we have operated, not independently but in support. This was brought out very, very carefully by the distinguished witnesses who appeared before our committee. Canada cannot act independently in wartime. We have acted in support. So long as our major allies, Britain and the United States, continue to have navy, army and air forces as separate identities, so Canada should have those separate identities in order that we may co-operate with them in wartime. We did it in the first war, in the second war and in Korea. In Korea our forces were brigaded with the Commonwealth division. That is quite proper; you do not operate alone. We operated with British troops in the first and second world wars, and on some occasions with American troops. But you do not operate alone.

These distinct forces should be maintained. I think this is an argument that you cannot get around, and it comes from the experience of our most distinguished service officers who gave evidence before the defence committee. What have we reached with regard to the utilization of our forces? This is where the Secretary of State for External Affairs enters upon the stage, because here is where the responsibility now rests. The Minister of National Defence has been going on his own, unchecked, untrammelled, and it is now time to rein him in and teach him some of the facts of life. The Secretary of State for External Affairs must give to this house, exactly and without his orotund phrases, a clear picture of what is Canada's external policy for the future.

Is the minister intending that we shall withdraw our troops from NATO? Is he intending that we shall just provide troops on demand from Canada by means of an airlift, if needed? Is he intending to discontinue the anti-submarine activities of our navy?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs knows better than the Minister of National Defence that there is still a threat from Russia. Russia has the largest submarine fleet in the world, and perhaps the largest fishing fleet. There will be danger off our shores unless we are prepared to be on guard. In Canadian naval circles and in United States naval circles this problem of protection against submarine threat is considered in its proper light. Why are we withdrawing from an anti-submarine role? Obviously we are, because we have fewer ships in service; we have not the men to man the ships that we have in service. So we are failing to maintain our commitment to NATO, by default.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs what he intends to do with regard to the proposition put forward by the Minister of National Defence on December 7 in relation to peace restoring. This is a phrase that is now being commonly used by writers. My parliamentary friend, the hon. member for Greenwood, loves this expression "peace restoring." I told him at a conference at Scarborough that I was going to accuse him of being a warmonger. Let us have a definition from the Secretary of State for External Affairs of the expression "peace restoring". I asked some of the distinguished gentlemen
14560	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment who appeared before us what they understood "peace restoring" to mean, and they said "We used to call that war". I think they are right because there is an implication in that phrase that there has been an engagement in war after which peace is restored. Therefore "peace restoring" is a very dangerous phrase to use.
At the time of the Korean war the then minister of national defence and the then secretary of state for external affairs, who is now the Prime Minister, spoke about aggression in Korea. I was only a backbencher at that time. Not much more attention has been paid to me up here in front than when I was sitting in the back benches, so I can alternate easily between the two. At that time I asked the government: Why do you not call it war rather than aggression? People were shooting at each other and being killed. Now we call it peace restoring.
I am all in favour of peace; I do not want to go to war again. But let us be clear as to what we are doing. Peace restoring means punitive action, it means fighting. If we are going to provide an armed force with sea transport, air transport, and all the offensive weapons for peace restoring, it means that we are providing a force for war. Is the United Nations going to ask us individually and alone to undertake a mission for them and engage in war? I do not think we would be so foolish as to do that; and yet this is the information that is spreading out across this country. This is what people are saying. I will paraphrase some of their statements, such as: Canada does not have to maintain a navy, an army and an air force; Canada does not have to support our allies in Europe or the United States; let us have a special mobile and well equipped force for peace restoring.
I submit that this is a force for war. The Secretary of State for External Affairs must be careful about this, because the Minister of National Defence is running away madly. He has the bit in his teeth and he does not know where he is going. Let us not desert our allies or get out of step with the rest of the world. I will ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question, which he does not have to answer now because if he starts to speak I will not get another chance. There is trouble in Aden. I suppose that people would call it a brushfire war. If the British withdraw, are we to send there a special Canadian force to put out that conflict? A large number of Canadian soldiers would be killed if we did so.

DEBATES	April 5, 1967
What is the situation in Somaliland? Is there a chance that a brushfire war may develop there? What about Nigeria, where some internal trouble is developing? We have to be careful about this. Putting out brushfire wars sounds simple, but it is not, really. If a war starts, is there not a danger of the larger nations intervening in some way? Are we to rush over like a fire brigade to put out a brushfire war? I cannot think of anything more dangerous. We might easily sacrifice the lives of 1,000 Canadians by getting involved in such a conflict. Surely our job is to work with the United Nations, in concert with our allies, as we did in Korea, but not separately and apart. If we are going to work in concert with our allies, we should have a force similar to theirs, a navy, an army and an air force. This is what I am suggesting.
On January 31 I held out an olive branch to the Minister of National Defence. Subsequently I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he had read my speech, but he had not got around to it as he had been reading something else. In my speech I suggested that we should get the best of both worlds. There is a great division of opinion in this country. A great many people, more numerous than is imagined, want our defence forces to be maintained as they are now. They want the history and tradition of these forces sustained. They do not want the identity of the Royal Canadian Navy or the Royal Canadian Air Force wiped out. Let us get the best of both worlds. We want to continue to play our part in the activities of the United Nations in a peacekeeping role. I emphasize that it should be peacekeeping-not the warfare of peace restoring, but peacekeeping. I suggested in that speech that we should organize a special force for that purpose. We should enlist men specially, or draw them by secondment from the armed forces and let them serve overseas. We should dress them in a bottle green uniform and create an elite force to carry out police duties. This is exactly what our representative at the United Nations is advocating now.
I intended to ask the minister during the question period whether he has now accepted the suggestion which I put forward on January 31. Let us continue our peace keeping activities, such as we have been doing for years under UN auspices, and let us do it by means of a special force. We have about 2,000 men abroad performing this special task in
April 5, 19S7	COMMONS
Cyprus and the Gaza Strip, men in the surveillance corps and in the minister's pet organization, the International Control Commission. All of this could be done by a special force, with special training in police and diplomatic activities, because their role would be different from that of the fighting forces. I will admit readily that a force of that nature would not be useful at the outbreak of a war because they would not be trained to fight. I submit that it should not be a large force. We could provide 3,000 to 5,000 young Canadian men for this task. Here would be a chance for young Canada to do something abroad under the auspices of the UN. This would not be a peace restoring mission, which means bloodshed and slaughter, but a peace keeping mission, which is being carried out at the present time by the armed forces of this country.
The peace keeping force which I am proposing should be enlisted, trained and disciplined under the direction of the Department of National Defence for this particular purpose. We would not then be involved in the affairs of some of the countries which do not want armed forces on their territory, and quite rightly so. Our armed forces would not be acting in such a capacity, but we would have a special force for peace keeping purposes. It would be lightly armed for protection, not aggressively armed as is the case in some countries now.
That is the suggestion I put forward on January 31. I said: Let us keep our defence forces as they are now, and let us create a special force for United Nations peace keeping purposes. Let us not break up our defence forces which are now being trained for a special purpose and let us not pretend that we will set them at the beck and call of the UN for peace restoring, which is war.
I suggest to the government that it should think this over. Let us not confuse the Canadian public. Let us not destroy our three fighting services and develop a special peace restoring force for the United Nations, and then fail to take any action. If we wish to get involved in war, we will have to take some specific action here in the House of Commons.
I will conclude with a plea to the Prime Minister. It is the Prime Minister who carries the greatest responsibility with regard to the defence of this country. He has people to assist him. He has the advice of the experienced Secretary of State for External Affairs, a man who has surveyed the world and who has been here a long time.

I do not exclude the possibility that in the future it may become feasible, and indeed I hope it will, to withdraw our forces from Europe and to make our entire contribution from bases in Canada. But such a course of action is neither feasible nor desirable at this moment, and certainly not by unilateral decision. I ask this house to consider what would be the consequences on other countries, for example the smaller countries in Europe which are bound to us, in the NATO alliance, if we were to take a decision on our own to withdraw without the opportunity for collective consideration and judgment. The concept of
peace keeping I think is now well accepted within the context of the charter; certainly no country knows more about peace keeping than Canada, a country that has participated in nearly every peace keeping project of the United Nations. We are currently contributing to United Nations peace forces in Cyprus and on the Israel-U.A.R. border. We also contribute to United Nations observer missions active on Israel's frontier with Syria, Jordan and Lebanon, and in Kashmir. We participate also in the international supervisory commissions in Indochina, the latter three of course not being creations of the United Nations but of the Geneva conference of 1954. Canada has contributed to all of the larger United Nations peace keeping efforts in the period since 1949, and indeed, as I said a moment ago, to almost all of the smaller missions as well.
We have found ourselves generally accepted in this role for many reasons-because, I suppose, we do not happen to be marked with old prejudices, because we have well trained and competent forces, and of course, because we have been willing participants. We have been willing because successive Canadian

National Defence Act Amendment governments-the government of which my hon. friend was a member as well as this government and other preceding governments-and, indeed, most Canadians I think, believe that the United Nations has an important role in maintaining the peace. Despite halting progress in establishing the effective authority of the UN, I think we are all agreed that in the long run the world's best hope is to equip the United Nations to stand unchallenged as the keeper of the peace.
We must work to that end, however discouraging at times the result seems to be- and how discouraging it is, right today, in the United Nations for the Canadian delegation in respect of its initiative to try to bring about a greater acceptance of collective responsibility in the financing and in the operational responsibilities of United Nations peace keeping.
There are some who would prefer that we should now devote the bulk, or even all, of our military forces solely to UN peace keeping duties. I think this proposition deserves critical examination, attractive though it may appear in the light of our longer range goal of co-operative international security. The United Nations is working with gradually increasing effectiveness to surmount the immense problems inherent in national rivalries, and in the social and economic injustices which give rise to world tensions. But there is still basic disagreement on what that organization can do with regard to the authorization, control and financing of peace keeping operations.
In co-operation with others, Canada is striving to reach a generally acceptable basis on which future operations can be undertaken, so that we shall not have to carry the kind of load which we are carrying, for instance, in Cyprus. Even if these questions are resolved there can be no assurance that the political consensus in the United Nations necessary to establish an effective peace keeping operation will in each case be attainable. This is particularly true for situations involving the major powers, let alone those involving a confrontation between them.
In these circumstances, there is really no present substitute for defensive arrangements among groups of nations. While we search and work for the ideal, we cannot discard the practical foundations of security. It would therefore be unwise to limit our contribution to the maintenance of peace and security solely to participate in UN peace keeping operations. To discontinue our commitments to continental and NATO defence now would

The unanimous decision by the chiefs of staff and all the staff members who considered it was that in the world today the least likely kind of war is an all out thermonuclear war. At the other end of the spectrum, the most likely kind of war is a continuation of small wars, riots, insurrections, the overthrow of civil government, namely, the kind of conflict that has been going on almost continuously throughout history and certainly continuously during the 20 years since world war II.
Each side in the cold war, the United States and the U.S.S.R., has sufficient thermonuclear striking power that even after one side had commenced a sneak attack the other would be able to retaliate, from hardened and dispersed bases, with sufficient power to wipe out the agressor's industrialized areas. Therefore this kind of attack would be irrational.
Then on the next page he continues his speech as follows:
Our problem in Canada was to devise and develop a defence policy sufficiently broad and with sufficient flexibility that our forces could contribute to the deterrence of a major war at one end of the scale and through to these peacekeeping activities at the other end of the scale or assist in putting out a small conflagration before it escalated into all-out thermonuclear war.
Let us consider the statement made by the Prime Minister on June 7, 1963 when he spoke about our new defence policy, the conventional role, and a new approach for Canada in collective alliances. Let us consider the words of the Minister of National Defence uttered here last Monday when he spoke about the best that Canada can supply, and when he said that it is irrational to think of a thermonuclear war because if one side starts it the other will be wiped out. In addition let us look at the statements made today, that we should meet our commitments with a new force. I ask the minister: What is the role of the Canadian armed forces? What was it, not only in the past, but what is it now when we are considering this bill and, in particular, what will it be in the future?-because now

DEBATES	April 5, 1967
we are being faced with a complete reorganization of the Canadian armed forces.
I find the stand taken by both the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence to be completely irrational. A few moments ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that we should keep our brigade and our air division in Europe, and yet the Minister of National Defence has stated previously that any sneak attack might develop into a thermonuclear war. Even if there is a conventional sneak attack, how will our brigade meet it? Will it meet it with the Honest John rocket with a nuclear warhead? How will our air division fly to meet it? Will it do so equipped with nuclear warheads? I am not one who says we should pull out of NATO completely, but in my own view I do not see any purpose in maintaining in Europe our brigade and our air division. If they are going to stay there, then we should think about it in the light of the reorganization of our forces. If they are not going to be kept there, then that might change our thinking on Bill C-243. I believe we should be equipped for anti-submarine warfare, and I believe that this is a vital role which we can play in NATO. That is my own personal view.
I believe we should reconsider our position in NORAD, when the new agreement comes up in 1968. We must adjust to what our position will be in ten years. Are we going to maintain our present commitments with Bomarcs, with nuclear warheads on our Canadian soil, with Voodoos with nuclear war-heads? If so, why? Let the minister state, as he has done so often, that in the case of a war it is not Canada which will be attacked but the United States, and that it will not be an all-out nuclear conflict. What is Canada doing to prepare for such an eventuality? I say, Mr. Chairman, that we should have some knowledge of the future role of the Canadian armed forces. Knowing that, we can then give proper consideration to this bill.
However, I should like to go beyond that. I cannot remember any witness who gave evidence before the committee, whether in the service or retired, who has opposed the policy of integration. I do not believe there is any member in the house who would basically oppose integration. The question is, where do we go from there? Also I cannot think of one witness who gave evidence before the committee who did not say that it would take from four to six years to implement integration, to test it and then to adjust it according to problems which cannot be foreseen now.
April 5, 1967	COMMONS
In view of this it is my own personal opinion that we could have avoided this discourse, and these arguments pro and con a single service, if the government had adopted a more sensible approach to this entire question, if it had emphasized the fact that it would take five to six years to put integration into effect, and if it had not insisted on the legalistic bill now before us authorizing the government to promulgate integration inside of four months.
The minister put himself in a poor position when he announced it will take five years to accomplish the first stage, and now wishes authorization for the next five or ten years. Surely we should go step by step, because if we try to jump all the way we might fall and break our necks. This would mean the disorganization and disruption of the Canadian armed forces. Ultimately our forces may become a single service, but why does the government have to ram it down the throats of members of parliament, of members of the armed services and of the people of Canada? The minister speaks of the single service concept and of full integration, but there will still have to be an army, a navy and an air force; there is no question about it.
If we accept full integration, what is wrong with letting those who honour the traditions of the service they joined to be known as members of the R.C.N., the R.C.A.F. or the army, in the integrated service? The government can have its integration, its command, its control, but what is so wrong with letting the services maintain their units and their designations within the integrated service? Surely that is not a fundamental change, and the government and the minister could have acceded to it, for psychological reasons if for no others.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The same thing applies to the common uniform. It applies also to the one-rank structure. Why should we be the only country in the world-at least of which I know-among our allies, where an admiral has to be a general or an air chief marshal has to be a general? Why should this be so? Perhaps this situation will evolve eventually, yes, but why bring it about now to cause confusion and heartbreak?
It is not good enough to say that the minister is taking the power under which he may make these designations, but that the government may hold it in abeyance. Once you have the power, God knows how it is going to be used. Why is it necessary to bring in this sort of thing? I am convinced that a little bit of
National Defence Act Amendment reason and compromise by the minister would have enabled us to go a long way toward meeting what he has in mind. I do want to reiterate that there is bound to be opposition when the minister says "This is it", and especially when we are not clear as to what the future role of our armed forces is to be. The government has placed many of us in a difficult position. We believe in progress; we believe in integration and we sincerely hope it can be made to work. Ultimately, it may lead to unification, a single service.
Then, we are led to ask, which comes first? From our point of view the policy and the rules come before the structure. If we can get the policy and the rules before the structure, then there might not be any question at all, beyond perhaps an odd change in a clause, and we could go right through this bill. If the minister and the government remain arrogant and say, "Play ball our way, or else," then in the last analysis we will have to decide on our course of action. If you cannot get a policy before a structure, then you must be getting a structure first, because the structure will force you to get a policy and an objective. It has to be one way or the other.
This is the position in which the government is placing the members of this house. We will have to make our decision according to what we believe is best for the armed forces and for Canada. From now until this bill is completed, the members of this party will maintain the principle that was enunciated by the hon. member for Greenwood, and which I have tried to enunciate, that no matter what happens we will vote on each clause according to whether we think it is good, bad or, indifferent in the over-all legislative picture. In the final analysis, we will search our consciences and vote in the way we think is right for the future of Canada.

speechtext:
I was a member, Mr. Chairman, of the defence committee and heard the testimony on this bill. The committee heard testimony on all sides of this particular question. I feel it is important to realize that, at least where the opposition is concerned, there are as many sides as there are witnesses opposed to this legislation. When dealing with this legislation and the testimony relating to it, it is necessary I believe to judge the merits of the evidence and the credibility of the individual witnesses who appeared. In so far as this bill is concerned, the committee could group those gentlemen who appeared before us into three categories. The first would be political, the second the
14574	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment serving officers and the third the retired officers.
Now, the individuals in each of these three categories have limitations in their ability to present evidence. The first group, the minister and associate minister, are obviously the most qualified in all areas, except perhaps expertise on specific points. The second group, service officers, complement the minister and associate minister by providing the expertise and opinions on military considerations, but must refrain from making statements on policy.
The testimony of the third group, the retired officers, is possibly the most difficult to weigh. In the committee, Mr. Chairman, we were faced with a very real dilemma, the credibility of this group of witnesses. The minister and the defence staff all gave comprehensive and corroborative testimony. Nowhere, I suggest, was there a contradiction, as will be indicated by the minutes of evidence. However, on the other side one finds it difficult to choose whom to believe, particularly when the conflict arises over what I suggest are the gut issues.
The relevance, credibility and merit of their evidence-I am speaking of the retired officers-is directly related to the positions they had while in the service, the length of time they have been out of the service and any bias that has resulted from their manner of leaving, their present political affiliations and their membership in or association with interested organizations. For the most part, these are men who have high rank and have given long and loyal service to their country.
However, Mr. Chairman, I ask, are they still in touch? We are all agreed that the study of defence matters is exceedingly difficult because of the pace of development and change, particularly in our Canadian setting, as a result of the present reorganization. I submit that these men no longer have available to them the plans, documents and sources of information that they had at one time. The new information they receive after leaving the service-and this came from the witnesses themselves-comes from news reports, which are not exactly the best source, and second or third hand from friends, who are presently serving officers. I might say that these are hardly adequate bases for judgment.
It is significant that many of them had not read the present bill but had prepared briefs on unification, and were quite willing and ready to answer questions on unification. This was their right, of course, and was what they

DEBATES	April 5, 1967
were there to do. Many admitted however they had not read the bill. The many briefs presented, and the supporting evidence, produced certain contradictions which I should like to put forward, Mr. Chairman. General Moncel stated that he wrote four plans for unification, and the one the minister selected was the one he rejected out of hand. This statement appears on page 1212 of the committee evidence.
Later, Air Chief Marshal Miller, then chief of defence staff and General Moncel's direct superior, through whom these plans would have been forwarded stated, in answer to a question I asked, that he had seen no such plans. General Allard, present chief of staff, stated that in so far as he knew, these plans never existed. He had made a search of the department. Significantly General Moncel, referring to his retirement later stated, "I left because I could not write such a plan."
Admiral Brock, speaking about the lack of knowledge on the part of serving officers in 1964 as to what was going on, said as recorded on page 959 of the evidence:
No one seemed for a single moment to believe that the one reference in the white paper could be anything but an odd expression.
Admiral Rayner put it quite succinctly when he said, as recorded on page 2011 of the
evidence:
I had no doubts of what a single unified service meant: I had always assumed it would be one service, with one uniform and a loss of identity to the three services we have now.
General Fleury, however, seemed to agree with Admiral Brock when he stated, as recorded on page 1315:
It was not clear to me and it was not clear to the vast majority of the people in the armed forces what was meant.
However, General Moncel stated-and I read from page 1310:
I was well aware of the fact that the white paper said that unification was the ultimate end.
There you have it, Mr. Chairman. One admiral and one general say they did not know and one admiral and one general categorically state they they did know. It is difficult for me to conceive of a deficiency of knowledge in high ranking serving officers in an issue so fundamental as this. It is my submission they must have known. Regarding communications, General Fleury said:
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Communications were very bad within the headquarters and between the commanders in the field.


General Moncel countered by stating that communications could not be simpler, that it is straightforward.
Later on, referring to the testimony of previous witnesses on the proposed reorganization, the hon. member for Edmonton West made this statement, as reported at page 1314 of the committee proceedings:
No serving officers at the time were asked to testify how they felt about this organization.
To this General Moncel replied:
If they said this, it is quite wrong. I sat on defence council and we heard lots of "chaps" giving vent to their views on It.
Admiral Landymore said that the new reenlistment program contained in the bill would be an invitation to trade unions in the armed forces. Again, General Moncel disagreed, saying that he could not believe what Admiral Landymore said would come true. When questioned by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek about Admiral Landymore's suggestion that, under provisions of the bill, the minister of defence could commit Canadian forces anywhere without consulting parliament, General Moncel said, as reported at page 1306:
I cannot believe it.
Many of the witnesses that appeared expressed the view that the troops were opposed to unification. As reported at page 1379, Air Marshal Annis said:
I believe our minister may be correct when he suggested that unification had large popularity within the Canadian armed forces.
To be fair to him, Mr. Chairman, he went on to characterize how this support was divided.
The list of contradictions goes on and on, Mr. Chairman. I have quoted these few examples to demonstrate the degree of the problem. On the one hand, we have the members of the present defence staff who agree to a man on all points in their testimony, including the opinion that unification is the right organization for the Canadian armed forces.
On the other hand, we have some retired officers, whose testimony is fraught with contradiction, who in the main agree on the principle of unification, but who disagree on different specific aspects with either the minister, the defence staff, other opposition witnesses, or in some cases even themselves. The important element in all their testimony is whether or not they agree with unification, regardless of the manner of implementation, and the
National Defence Act Amendment consensus is a resounding vote in favour of unification. But, Mr. Chairman, as I have stated, some of them had not read the bill, nor had they heard or read the briefs of the defence staff. It is also significant that most of the discussion centred on the success of integration. of which of course they were all in favour, as that was the stage in which they were involved. If they were speaking of some of the difficulties which were being experienced with integration, they had solutions to offer.
The world is following our lead in integrating the armed services-

speechtext:
-but what of unification? Somebody says "oh", but it is a fact that this is so. We hear comments like: "We should not do it until somebody else does". "It has not been tried and it is not proven". "We are too small to try something like this". "Let the United States or Britain try it first. If it works-and I am certain it would-let us jump on the band wagon and follow their lead".
Most of these witnesses, Mr. Chairman, with one or two significant exceptions, were not opposed to the principle of unification. They were, however, opposed to doing it now, and for the most part their testimony was directed to that end. In effect, they said: Let us wait a few years and then we will go ahead.
General Foulkes, who was, in effect, an opposition witness, pretty well summed up this attitude when he said, as reported at page 1228:
In 1963 when I was here I think I remarked that the attitude of the chiefs was "Yes, we believe in integration but please do not do it while I am here."
He is speaking of integration, not unification. He went on:
"I do not want to be known as the chief of staff who ruined these services". This was the hatural attitude of an officer who had come all the way up through the service, who was responsible for the welfare of the service and not only to those in the service, but to the institutions which supported it. Although they all supported it, they were not so keen to go ahead with it during their tenure of office.
Perhaps these men are not so keen now to go ahead with it during their term of retirement, and I suggest probably for the same reason as that referred to by General Foulkes. But the members of the present defence staff are prepared to go ahead.

National Defence Act Amendment
General Allard stated to the committee, during his appearance before them on February 28 last, that in making his presentation he did so as the man responsible for carrying out the policy of the government, through the Minister of National Defence, for ensuring that the defence forces that we have today are organized, equipped, trained and possess the morale to accept any task they have or are likely to be given. He said he felt absolutely confident that this task can be carried out best by the reorganization of the forces as set out in Bill No. C-243.
I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that a man with the background, experience and service record of General Allard could make such a statement if he did not believe in it.
I would now like to deal with the fallacious statement-and it is a fallacious statement-by some hon. gentlemen opposite and some witnesses that unification is proceeding ahead too fast. When making these completely inaccurate statements, it is obvious that they have not listened to the expert testimony of witnesses before the committee. On Tuesday, February 7, 1967, at our very first meeting, we heard a two-hour brief by Air Marshal F. R. Sharp, vice-chief of the defence staff, and a major portion of that brief was directed to the time schedule for unification. I know it has been quoted before, but I should like to quote one paragraph of the vice chief's brief:
Because this is a very complex job, very thorough and careful planning is required. The department has, on the one hand, been accused of acting too quickly, that is, not doing sufficient planning, and, on the other hand, of not deciding sooner the details of what is involved in unification. Since planning takes time and since the details cannot be decided and divulged until the planning has been completed, it is obvious that the department cannot satisfy both of these criticisms. To take time for adequate planning means that there will be some delay before the details of unification can be announced. To quickly announce the details implies inadequate planning. However, to postpone the decision to unify until all the details have been worked out is contrary to common sense.
Here, Mr. Chairman, we are faced with the most challenging and exciting concept in modern military organization, and what do the opponents use as arguments? They engage in picayune discussion, based on unwillingness to accept the testimony of the only men-let me repeat, the only men-who are in a position to know what the proper time phase is, namely the present serving officers on the defence staff.
DEBATES	April 5, 1967
Air Marshal Sharp told us that planning for unification has been going on since 1964 and that it will not be completed until 1971 at the earliest. That, Mr. Chairman, adds up to a seven year program. Certainly, in this day and age it is time we realized that we can no longer afford to "wait and see" indefinitely; that we cannot simply put off our decisions for three years or five years because of the outcry of a small nostalgic group fighting for the preservation of an expensive, outdated and inefficient system of military organization. They are not looking for a pause for three or five years; they are looking for a permanent halt to the modernization of Canada's military establishment.
The Air Marshal's presentation illustrated with charts the program planning and scheduling. He indicated that to accomplish the aims of unification involved about 500 complex, interlocking stages and that progress or delays in one program had consequent effects on several others.
The minister and the defence staff have continuously stressed one point in the discussions both in and out of the committee, and it is that Bill C-243 is the final phase of the integration-unification cycle. Integration and unification are not neatly defined packages-and this was a point made by many witnesses, even those in opposition. They are not independent entities. Rather they are interlocking and interdependent stages in an over-all scheme designed to give Canada the best fighting force per tax dollar the world has ever seen.
General Allard told the committee that he has had to stop many programs that were impinging on unification, as the armed forces do not yet have the authority to complete their programs without the passing of this bill. To me, and to many of us, this indicates that planning and execution are well on schedule, and that the only part of the program that is behind schedule is the passing of the necessary legislation.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Much ado has been made about something called "instant unification". Some people seem to think that a stroke of the pen proclaiming this legislation will declare the process complete. This utter nonsense, as is shown by the opening statement of the minister. When this bill has been passed and proclaimed, it will do one thing and one thing alone-it will give the men and women of our Canadian armed forces the legal right to continue with

April 5, 1967	COMMONS
the necessary final planning and to begin to implement the plan. Bill C-243 is simply permissive legislation-nothing more, nothing less.
General Allard, chief of the defence staff, said this:
I would refer to the question regarding any suspension or delay in proceeding with the final stage of re-organization-unification. I sincerely believe a postponement or delay in starting this final stage would have a most serious effect on all of us now serving and on our recruiting prospects. What the serviceman is saying to us now is this, "Get on with it", and in my opinion any delay-one year, two years, five years or even a few months-would seriously impair morale.
This proposal is not designed to cope with the past, it is for the present and the future.
It is warming to note that General Worthington in an article published in the Ottawa Journal of Tuesday, April 4, says the same thing. I continue quoting General Allard:
I am convinced that not only is it right-but that it will appeal to the youth of today and tomorrow. The idea of a single force, in a single, distinctively Canadian uniform-working, living, training and, most important, thinking together as one entity-is an exciting and challenging idea. After all, it is designed to meet the problems of a modern world-a scientific world-which is growing away beyond the barriers of the past at a speed that cannot stand the slow pace of yesterday.
Now come these important words:
For all this-you know that we do not intend to proceed in haste-but rather in a carefully planned manner which will extend over a number of years. All that is required now is the authority to do so.
Those are the words of General Allard. Air Marshall Annis agreed that he was not opposed to the end result, integration into one single force, one rank, one uniform. General Foulkes said:
The problem can only be solved by complete unification of the three services with one Chief of Staff, one chain of command, one ladder of promotion and one uniform.
General Moncel said:
I was well aware of the fact that the white paper said that unification was the ultimate end. Well, that was fine. There was nothing wrong with it as a name.
I ask you, are these the statements of men who are opponents of unification? Again I reiterate, the important element of all the testimony in opposition is whether or not they agree with unification, regardless of the manner of implementation; and as stated earlier, the consensus is a resounding vote in favour of unification.
National Defence Act Amendment
When we look at the bill in this, its proper perspective, and examine the testimony of the witnesses who have seemingly opposed it, we find for the most part that there is really very little ground for contention. The major theme of these witnesses and of hon. gentlemen opposite has been "It's a good thing, but let's wait a few years before we do it."
Mr. Chairman, that is not a sound argument. The plan will not be implemented fully until 1972 at the earliest. Simple arithmetic shows that 1972 is five years away, and that we have already had three years of planning behind us. The minister and the defence staff are not rushing headlong into this, I submit. They are not moving at great speed as General Moncel said, "on an uncharted course toward a dim destination". I doubt whether he himself believes this. Rather, I submit they are moving at a controlled rate on a carefully planned program toward a concept necessitated by the technological revolution of the twentieth century and, perhaps more important, by the personal needs and welfare of Canada's serving men and women.
What is needed is enabling legislation now, so that they can get on with the planning and erase the uncertainty among our servicemen. It is now mainly the uncertainty concerning whether we are or are not going to unify that is bothering the servicemen, not the fact of unification itself.
We are here as parliamentarians, Mr. Chairman, to carry out the will of the Canadian people and to act in the best interests of our country. In so doing we are always faced with opposition viewpoints. We have long recognized that this is a good thing. Our parliamentary system is composed of two elements-Her Majesty's loyal government and Her Majesty's loyal opposition, and although there are times when members on this side of the house may feel that hon. members opposite take their task of opposing too much to heart, we would still not wish to see the form of our legislative body changed. This is all to say that, no matter what the issue, no matter what the time, there will always be opposition to every proposal because, as the expression goes, "You can't please all of the people all of the time."
With regard to unification, it would be easy for us to say, "Let's wait a few years" and put it off, just as it would have been easy for the present Minister of National Defence to bask in the successes of integration and to leave the more difficult part of the job to his successor. But no one who is a member of this


Business of the House
house will remain so for long if he always takes the easy way out. As members of parliament we must have the courage of our convictions, and having recognized our duty we must carry it out. Our duty now, I submit, is to pass this bill, to make Canada's defence force stronger and more able to do the tasks it will be called upon to perform. Let us get on with it and take our place in the vanguard of forward thinking nations.
